entries.proposition: THIS SOURCE IS SCOPED TO INTRAVENTRICULAR DELIVERY, NOT INTRATHECAL DELIVERY, CONTRARY TO THE TITLE UNDER WHICH IT WAS ASSIGNED; ROUTE IS THE VARIABLE THE READING SET WAS ASSEMBLED TO SEPARATE FROM DOSE.
entries.snippet: The appreciation of these effects on CSF circulation will help predict variability in the intraventricular delivery of viral vectors and other biopharmaceuticals and inform the design of preclinical studies and clinical trials.
entries.anchor: Diseases affecting CSF flow, 'Actionable guidance for intraventricular dosing in preclinical studies and clinical trials'

entries.proposition: THE REVIEW STATES THAT FIXED DOSING ACROSS A POPULATION IS CURRENT PRACTICE AND THAT A CSF ROUTE REQUIRES INDIVIDUALISED CONSIDERATION OF PATHWAY PATENCY AND VENTRICULAR VOLUME INSTEAD.
entries.snippet: In the case of intraventricular therapies, dosing considerations may need to include factors such as the patency of the pathways and estimated ventricular volume (at a minimum), much as a pediatric dosing schedule is adjusted according to weight.
entries.anchor: Additional factors in physiological CSF flow variability, 'Effects of age and sex on CSF flow'

entries.proposition: AGE IS NAMED BY THE AUTHORS AMONG THE TOP THREE DRIVERS OF VARIABILITY IN DELIVERED DOSE AT TARGET.
entries.snippet: According to a synthesis of the currently available literature, the most significant factors expected to cause variability of CSF macrocirculation would be overall CSF production, anatomical pathway variation, and age.
entries.anchor: Additional factors in physiological CSF flow variability, synthesis

entries.proposition: PAEDIATRIC CSF DYNAMICS CHANGE RAPIDLY WITH AGE, AND THE DETAIL IS DEFERRED BY THE AUTHORS TO A SUPPLEMENT THAT IS NOT PART OF THE BODY AND WAS NOT RETRIEVED.
entries.snippet: A more detailed consideration of CSF flow dynamics in the pediatric population is provided in Supplementary Material 2.
entries.anchor: Additional factors in physiological CSF flow variability, 'Effects of age and sex on CSF flow'

entries.proposition: A PATIENT-MEASURABLE, NON-TERMINAL ROUTE TO QUANTIFYING HOW MUCH VECTOR REACHES THE TARGET EXISTS IN PRINCIPLE THROUGH ISOTOPE-LABELLED CAPSID IMAGING; THE REVIEW CITES IT RATHER THAN DEMONSTRATING IT.
entries.snippet: More recently, antibodies and AAV9 capsids (as examples) can be labeled with PET isotopes such as carbon-11, fluorine-18, and zirconium-89, enabling noninvasive tracking and quantitative biodistribution studies in vivo, including after intraventricular administration (Pandit-Taskar et al., 2019; Allen et al., 2022; Bansal et al., 2025).
entries.anchor: Diseases affecting CSF flow, 'Direct assessment of the movement of therapeutic agents through the CSF'

entries.proposition: THE REVIEW CARRIES, AS A CITED PATTERN AND NOT AS ITS OWN MEASUREMENT, THAT VECTOR-ASSOCIATED DORSAL ROOT GANGLION TOXICITY IS MOST SEVERE AND CONSISTENT IN THE LUMBOSACRAL GANGLIA IN PRIMATE STUDIES.
entries.snippet: CSF-administered or peripheral-blood-administered viral vectors are known to present a risk of inducing DRG toxicity (Hinderer et al., 2018; Hawley et al., 2025), which tends to be most severe and consistent in the lumbosacral DRGs in non-human primate studies (Buss et al., 2022).
entries.anchor: Anatomy of the CSF pathways, 'Spinal pathways'
